note.text: Your skull is a hard case of bone that protects your brain.

steps.title: Spine
steps.instruction: Trace the spine down the middle.

note.text: Your spine, or backbone, is a stack of small bones. It holds your body up and protects the spinal cord inside it.

steps.title: Ribs
steps.instruction: Trace the four ribs on each side.

note.text: Your ribs form a cage around your chest. It protects your heart and lungs. Most people have 12 pairs; we've drawn 4.
note.remember: Rib cage protects heart and lungs.

steps.title: Arm bones
steps.instruction: Draw the two collarbones, then the upper and lower bones of each arm.

note.text: Your arms hang from your collarbones at the shoulders. Muscles pull on the arm bones to move them, so you can lift, throw and write.

steps.title: Pelvis
steps.instruction: Trace the pelvis, or hip bones.

note.text: The pelvis connects your legs to your body. It's built to be steady, so it can support your weight when you stand and walk.

steps.title: Leg bones
steps.instruction: Draw both legs: the thigh bones, then the shin bones.

note.text: The thigh bone, or femur, is the longest and strongest bone in your body. It's about a quarter of your height.
Each kneecap sits in front of the knee joint, where the thigh bone meets the shin bone.

steps.title: Label the bones
steps.instruction: Pick the right name for each numbered bone.

targets.role: Supports the body; protects the spinal cord.
Connects the legs to the body.

mistakes.Shin bone: The shin bone is below the knee. Above it is the femur, the thigh bone.

commonMistakes.Heart: The heart isn't a bone: it's a muscle, protected by the ribs.

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: Which bones protect the organs you need to breathe?

options.feedback: Yes. The rib cage surrounds the lungs, and the heart beside them.
The skull protects the brain. The ribs protect the lungs.
The femur is the thigh bone: it holds you up. The ribs protect the lungs.
The pelvis connects your legs. The rib cage protects your lungs.

steps.title: Fun fact
steps.question: A baby is born with about 300 bones, but an adult has 206. What happens to the rest?

options.text: Some of them fuse, growing together into one bone
options.feedback: Right. As babies grow, some bones join together. That's how 270 to 300 bones become 206.

options.text: They fall out like baby teeth
options.feedback: Bones don't fall out. Some of them grow together, or fuse.
Bones stay bone. Some of them join together as you grow.

options.text: Babies don't really have more bones
options.feedback: They do: about 270 to 300. Some fuse together over time.
